question: When a machine takes over a job's name and its routine tasks, as computers did to human computers and programmers, can the newest workers still find a way to learn and move on to the work that remains?

issues.note: The cut from the warm interior of the computing room to a dusk street with a lamplighter has a lower-third caption ('same word - three different jobs') that disappears abruptly. The lamplighter figure is a tiny silhouette and the link between lamplighter and computer is not yet clear.

The jump from the 1950s office to a dark, empty archive corridor for 'the second kind of work' has no visual hook. The caption flickers in only at +2.5 s, and the corridor does not obviously show programming.

The narration says 'two job titles' while the picture is still the single programmer desk with the 'computer programmers' label. The second title, software developers, comes later at T12, so the picture lags the narration.

The split-screen (Langley 1940s / today) reuses the desk imagery to say 'checking the machine's numbers: an old job here'. It then cuts to a dim, wide, empty office for 'the people just starting out', and that shot does not show beginners.

After the ladder and dark-floor shot for 'where will the next beginners learn?', the film jumps straight to the dusk street. The caption 'What happens to a job when a machine takes its name?' is a new question that is not tied to the preceding thought.

The 'Women computers at the Langley laboratory' pictogram chart (75 women) sits abruptly between a historical photo and a 3D office, and its figures are small. It is a style break from the rest of the film.
The BLS quote card sits on screen for about 8 s, and the text hardly changes between the two frames.
The card with 'Programming is one of many work activities...' stays up for roughly 8 to 12 s over several frames, with little new to look at.
The dim, empty office is reused many times in the section on young workers (R15.6 to R17.2, R17.3 to R17.4), so the picture hardly changes across a long stretch of statistics narration.
The same dim open-plan office angle repeats across R16.5 to R17.4 while the captions change but the picture does not.
